title: Breadth-first search (BFS), levels and paths
overview: BFS explores a graph layer by layer from a source using a queue. Because it reaches nodes in order of distance, the same code also gives the shortest number of edges to every node (its level) and, with a parent array, the actual shortest path. These patterns come back in almost every later graph problem.

concepts.explain: Push the source, mark it visited. Repeatedly pop the front node and push every unvisited neighbour, marking it visited **when it is pushed** so it never enters the queue twice.
Set `level[src] = 0` and `level[child] = level[par] + 1`. In an unweighted graph this is the fewest edges from the source.
Store `parent[child] = par` when a child is discovered. Walking `parent` back from the destination gives the path in reverse.
After one BFS, `vis[x]` tells whether `x` can be reached from the source at all.
`memset(vis, false, ...)` and `memset(level, -1, ...)` before each BFS; `-1` means "not reached". `memset` needs `<cstring>`.
Every node is pushed once and every edge is looked at once (twice when undirected): O(V + E).

files.title: BFS traversal
files.what: Builds an undirected graph and prints the nodes in the order BFS visits them from node 0.
steps: Read the edges into `adj_list` (both directions).
Clear `visited` with `memset`, then call `bfs(0)`.
In `bfs`, push `src` and mark it visited.
Pop the front node `par`, print it, and push each unvisited `child`, marking it right away.
The loop ends when the queue is empty: every reachable node was printed once.
files.input_note: `n e`, then `e` edges. BFS always starts from node 0.
files.output_note: `0 1 2 3 4 5`: first 0, then its neighbours 1 and 2, then their neighbours 3 and 4, then 5.
files.watch_out: Tip: on some compilers you need `#include <cstring>` for `memset`; this file relies on another header bringing it in.

check.q: Why mark a node visited when it is pushed instead of when it is popped?
check.a: Otherwise the same node could be pushed several times by different parents before it is popped.

files.title: Shortest distance with BFS levels
files.what: Adds a `level` array to BFS so that after one run it knows the distance (in edges) from the source to every node.
steps: Read the graph, then `src` and `dest`.
Set all `level` to `-1` (unreached) and `level[src] = 0`.
When a child is discovered: `level[child] = level[par] + 1`.
BFS still prints its visiting order, then the program prints `level of dest`.
files.input_note: `n e`, the edges, then one line `src dest`.
files.output_note: `0 1 2 3 4 5 level of 5 = 3`: the BFS order, then the answer 3 (path 0-1-3-5).
files.watch_out: Tip: on some compilers you need `#include <cstring>` for `memset`; this file relies on another header bringing it in.

check.q: What does `level[x] == -1` mean after the BFS?
check.a: Node `x` cannot be reached from the source.

files.title: Can we reach a node?
files.what: Runs BFS from `src` and answers YES if `dest` got visited.
steps: Build the graph, read `src` and `dest`.
Run `bfs(src)`; it marks every reachable node in `visited`.
If `visited[dest]` is true print YES, otherwise NO.
files.input_note: `n e`, edges, then `src dest`. Here 0 and 2 are in the same piece; 4-5 is a separate piece.
files.output_note: `0 1 3 2 YES << endl`: the BFS order and then the answer (with a stray ` << endl` in the text, see Watch out).
files.watch_out: The quotes are misplaced: `cout << "YES << endl";` prints the text ` << endl` literally. Write `cout << "YES" << endl;`. Tip: on some compilers you need `#include <cstring>` for `memset`; this file relies on another header bringing it in.

check.q: After a BFS from `s`, how do you test if `t` is reachable in O(1)?

files.title: Print the shortest path
files.what: Records each node's `parent` during BFS, then walks back from the destination to print the path, first reversed and then in the right order.
steps: Set `parent` to `-1` for all nodes (the source keeps -1).
When a child is discovered: `parent[child] = par`.
Way 1: start at `dest`, print `node`, move to `parent[node]` until you hit -1. This is dest → src.
Way 2: collect the same nodes in a vector `path`, `reverse` it, then print src → dest.
files.output_note: Everything on one line: `0 1 2 3 4 5` (BFS order), `5 3 1 0` (reversed path), `0 1 3 5` (correct path).
files.watch_out: The three prints have no line breaks between them, so add `cout << endl;` to read them easily. Tip: on some compilers you need `#include <cstring>` for `memset`; this file relies on another header bringing it in.

check.q: Why does the backward walk stop?
check.a: The source's parent is -1, and the loop runs while `node != -1`.

files.title: Many shortest-distance queries
files.what: For each query `(S, D)` it runs a fresh BFS from S and prints the level of D (or -1).
steps: Build the graph once.
For each query, `bfs(src)` first resets `visited` and `level` itself.
After the BFS, `level[dest]` is the answer (-1 if unreachable).
files.input_note: `n e`, edges, `Q`, then Q lines `S D`.
files.output_note: Each line starts with the BFS order (a leftover debug print) and ends with the answer: `level of 5 = 2`, `level of 5 = 3`, `level of 0 = 0`. The judge expects only `2`, `3`, `0`.
files.watch_out: For the judge, remove the `cout << par` debug line and print only `level[dest]`. Tip: on some compilers you need `#include <cstring>` for `memset`; this file relies on another header bringing it in.

check.q: Why must `visited` and `level` be reset for every query?
check.a: Each query uses a different source; old marks would stop the new BFS from visiting nodes.

files.title: Nodes at level L
files.what: BFS from node 0 and collects every node whose level equals L, then prints them in descending order.
steps: Run BFS from 0 while computing `level`.
When a node is popped, if `level[par] == l` push it into `nodes`.
Sort `nodes` with `greater<int>()` and print.
files.complexity: Time O(V + E + k log k) · Space O(V)
files.output_note: `L = 1` prints `3 2 1`: the three neighbours of 0, largest first.
files.watch_out: Tip: on some compilers you need `#include <cstring>` for `memset`; this file relies on another header bringing it in.

check.q: How do you sort a vector in descending order?

files.title: Count direct neighbours
files.what: No search needed: the number of nodes directly connected to N is the size of its adjacency list.
steps: Build the adjacency list.
Read `node`.
Print `adj_list[node].size()`.
files.complexity: Time O(V + E) to build, O(1) per answer
files.output_note: The output `3` means node 1 touches three nodes (0, 2 and 3).

check.q: What is `adj_list[x].size()` called in graph language?

files.title: LeetCode 841 - Keys and Rooms
files.what: Rooms are nodes and keys are directed edges. BFS from room 0; if every room gets visited, the answer is true.
steps: `rooms[i]` is already an adjacency list: the keys found in room i.
`bfs(0, rooms)` visits every room we can unlock.
Loop over all rooms; if any `vis[i]` is false, return false.
Otherwise return true.
files.complexity: Time O(n + total keys) · Space O(n)
files.input_note: Test driver format: number of cases; for each: `n`, then n lines `k key1 .. keyk`. These are LeetCode's two examples.
files.output_note: `true` then `false`, which match LeetCode's expected answers (in example 2, room 2's only key is locked inside room 2).

check.q: Why is this a graph problem even though the word graph never appears?
check.a: Rooms are nodes and a key in room a for room b is an edge a → b; the question is whether all nodes are reachable from 0.

recap: BFS = queue + visited; mark when you push.
`level[child] = level[par] + 1` gives shortest distance in unweighted graphs.
`parent[child] = par` lets you rebuild the path; reverse it at the end.

check_yourself.q: Why does BFS give shortest distances only when all edges have the same weight?
check_yourself.a: It counts edges layer by layer; with different weights a path with more edges can be cheaper.

check_yourself.q: A BFS from node 0 never reaches node 7. What are `level[7]` and `parent[7]`?
check_yourself.a: Both stay at their start value, -1.

check_yourself.q: What data structure turns BFS into DFS if you swap it in?
check_yourself.a: A stack (LIFO) instead of a queue (FIFO).
